ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study protocol was fully reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board for Psychological Research (Egyesített Pszichológiai Kutatásetikai Bizottság [EPKEB]; Approval Number: 2022-127).
All procedures performed in this study involving human participants were in accordance with the ethical standards of the institutional research committee and with the Helsinki Declaration.
All participants were native Hungarian speakers with no reported history of hearing impairment, learning disabilities, speech-language disorders, or neurological conditions.
Prior to the experiment, informed written consent was obtained from both the participating children and their parents or legal guardians.
Participants were presented with lists of frequent words, rare words, and pseudowords across three blocks.
Participants completed distinct conditions consisting of separate blocks for letters, numbers, and pictures of familiar, high-frequency objects (e.g., fish, chair, dog).
Participants were instructed to read the sentences aloud at a natural pace; a new sentence appeared immediately after they finished reading the current one.
Participants were instructed to repeat each sentence aloud after the auditory playback.

Relatedly, because participants were already literate, their orthographic knowledge may have influenced performance on the phonological awareness measures themselves, rather than these measures reflecting a pre-literate skill (Castles & Coltheart, 2004, as cited in Critten et al., 2021).

Assuming a standard acceptable misfit (RMSEA = .08) and an alpha level of .05, the statistical power to reject a misspecified model with 7 degrees of freedom was low (1 -β = .16). Further sensitivity analysis indicated that with N = 56, the current model only achieves adequate power (80%) to reliably detect large effect sizes (RMSEA ≥ .193). Consequently, while the descriptive fit indices suggest an excellent model fit, the non-significant chi-square statistic should be interpreted with caution due to limited statistical power, which reinforces the exploratory nature of investigating these structural relationships.

The path model demonstrated an excellent fit to the data. The chi-square test was non-significant, indicating that the model did not significantly deviate from the observed data structure (χ²(7) = 7.97, p = .335). Furthermore, all indices indicated excellent model fit (CFI = .995, TLI = .985, RMSEA = .050, SRMR = .054). Given the small sample size, a post-hoc power and sensitivity analysis was conducted using the semPower package (Moshagen & Bader, 2024) to evaluate the model's capacity to detect misspecifications.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the size of the current sample limits the statistical power available for detecting smaller effects, particularly within the path model, and constrains the generalizability of the pathway structure. As confirmed by sensitivity analysis, a sample size of 56 children only provides adequate statistical power to reliably detect large structural misspecifications (RMSEA ≥ .193). Consequently, the path model may lack the precision needed to capture smaller, yet theoretically meaningful pathways among the multiple cognitive and acoustic predictors. Therefore,conclusions regarding the unique contribution of each prosodic marker and the specific indirect role of phonological awareness should be considered exploratory and require validation in adequately powered future cohorts.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps < .01", "ps < .05", "ps > .05", 
"p < .01"), Text = c("While univariate Shapiro-Wilk tests indicated minor deviations from normality for two of the temporal prosodic metrics (Tempo Stability and Pausal Intrusions; ps < .01), a multivariate Shapiro-Wilk test confirmed that the assumption of multivariate normality for the overall dataset was not significantly violated (W = 0.971, p = .065).", 
"Rapid Automatized Naming (RAN) showed negative correlations with all four prosodic competence scores (rs = -.30 to -.42, all ps < .05), indicating that slower naming speed was associated with greater prosodic disruption during reading.", 
"Residual normality was confirmed for Pausal Intrusions and Melody Error (Shapiro-Wilk ps > .05), while minor deviations were detected for Tempo Stability (W = 0.951, p = .029) and Rhythm Error (W = 0.946, p = .020).", 
"PA = Phonological Awareness; RAN = Rapid Automatized Naming; DTW = Dynamic Time Warping. * p < .05. p < .01. *** p < .001."
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

text.text: Purpose: The development of reading fluency relies on phonological skills and prosodic competence, but evidence about the underlying mechanisms and concurrent relationships supporting this link remain scarce.
Previous research has relied on subjective rating scales or adult-based acoustic comparisons, mostly in stress-timed languages.

This study investigated whether objective acoustic markers of oral reading prosody serve as a potential link in the relationship between cognitive skills (phonological awareness [PA] and rapid automatized naming [RAN]) and reading fluency in a syllable-timed language.
Method: The sample consisted of 56 typically developing, Hungarian-speaking primary school children (Mage = 8.96 years, 55.36% boys) who completed standardized cognitive assessments.

Prosodic competence was measured by comparing acoustic features from an oral reading task against each child's own prosodic imitation baseline, using dynamic time warping to align melodic and rhythmic contours.
Data were analyzed using path analysis.
Results: Temporal features, especially tempo stability, emerged as the strongest predictor of reading fluency, whereas melodic and rhythmic markers added no unique variance.

Path analysis revealed that RAN predicted reading fluency directly, while PA's contribution was entirely indirect: stronger PA reduced pausal intrusions, which maintained temporal stability and, through it, reading fluency.
Conclusion: PA appears to be linked to reading fluency indirectly through sequential, temporal prosodic execution.

In the context of Hungarian (a syllable-timed language), sentence-level temporal mechanisms may carry the primary explanatory weight, highlighting that reading development models should account for the specific rhythmic properties of the reader's native language.

Reading fluency is the ability to read text quickly, accurately and with proper expression (Miller & Schwanenflugel, 2008; Benjamin & Schwanenflugel, 2010; Sarris & Dimakos, 2015), integrating lower-level decoding and higher-level comprehension processes (Duong et al., 2011).

text.text: The present study investigates whether acoustic dimensions of reading prosody account for the shared variance in the link between cognitive precursors and reading fluency in Hungarian primary school children.

Phonological awareness (PA), the ability to identify, manipulate, and analyze the sound structure of spoken words (syllables, onset-rime units, phonemes), is strongly associated with reading development (Calet et al., 2015; Holliman et al., 2017; Wade-Woolley & Heggie, 2016).

At the foundation of this scaffolding is suprasegmental phonology: the ability to identify and manipulate stress, timing, and intonation across syllables (Holliman et al., 2010; Calet et al., 2015; Holliman et al., 2017).

text.text: Hungarian occupies a distinctive position: it is syllable-timed with predictable, fixed initial stress, and neither pitch nor stress is lexically contrastive.
As recent acoustic research demonstrates, stress contrasts are notably weaker in Hungarian than in stress-timed languages.

The cognitive weight of prosodic processing is therefore expected to shift away from the word level; sentence-level prosody, specifically temporal execution, rhythmic phrasing, and pausing, should emerge as the primary suprasegmental mechanism supporting syntactic parsing and reading fluency.

Previous acoustic approaches have mostly correlated a child's prosodic contour with an adult model of the same sentence (Duong et al., 2011), which may not capture the natural variability in children's speech rate.

text.text: The present study instead benchmarks each child's oral reading against their own imitation of the same sentence, produced in a separate Prosodic Imitation Task (see Method), with the two aligned using dynamic time warping (DTW).

During data collection, four children were excluded due to extensive missing data across the experimental tasks.
Following these exclusions, the core sample consisted of fifty-six participants (Mage = 8.96 years; SD = 0.54; 31 boys) who completed the prosodic assessments.
We utilized the Hungarian adaptation of the Dyslexia Differential Diagnosis Maastricht Test battery (3DM-H; Tóth et al., 2014).
text.formatted: We utilized the Hungarian adaptation of the Dyslexia Differential Diagnosis Maastricht Test battery (3DM-H; <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Tóth et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The complete diagnostic battery contains 11 tests designed to assess cognitive processes essential for reading and spelling.

For the purposes of the present study, only three subtests were included in the current analyses due to their direct relevance to the study's focus, namely Reading Fluency, Phonological Awareness (PA) and Rapid Automatized Naming (RAN).
The Reading Fluency subtest measures the speed and accuracy of word decoding.
Participants were presented with lists of frequent words, rare words, and pseudowords across three blocks.
Within each block, items appeared on the screen in three vertical columns, with 15 items displayed simultaneously.
Children were instructed to read the words aloud column-by-column as quickly and accurately as possible.
The examiner manually advanced the screen as soon as the child finished reading the visible words, allowing a new set of 15 items to appear.
The task continued until the child completed all 75 items in the block or the 30-second time limit elapsed.
Age-standardized fluency scores including both speed and accuracy measures generated by the 3DM-H software were used as the outcome measure.
Phonological Awareness was assessed using the Phoneme Deletion subtest.
In this task, participants heard pseudowords through headphones and were asked to repeat the item while omitting a specific target phoneme (e.g., saying the pseudoword "hilm" without the "m" sound).
The task comprised 27 test items divided into three blocks of increasing complexity, evaluating the deletion of initial, final, and internal consonants.
The examiner recorded response accuracy, and the software logged reaction times to compute the age-standardized PA scores used in the analyses.
The Rapid Automatized Naming subtest evaluated the speed of visual-verbal processing and lexical retrieval.
Participants completed distinct conditions consisting of separate blocks for letters, numbers, and pictures of familiar, high-frequency objects (e.g., fish, chair, dog).
Within each block, 15 stimuli from the same category were displayed simultaneously, organized into three vertical columns on the screen.
Children were required to name the items aloud, column-by-column, as rapidly as possible.
The examiner recorded the total completion time required to name all items within each category.
Age-standardized speed scores computed by the 3DM-H software served as the final RAN outcome measure.
To evaluate prosodic execution, we designed a custom Prosodic Reading Task (PRT) and Prosodic Imitation Task (PIT).
All stimuli comprised everyday, age-appropriate utterances familiar to children.
Sentence length was controlled, ranging from 1 to 7 words (M = 3.85) and from 2 to 15 syllables (M = 7.65).
Although the two tasks were designed to be symmetrical with a total pool of 30 sentences, omissions during data collection resulted in one missing item per task.
Consequently, each task contained 29 sentences, 28 of which were identical across both conditions to ensure direct acoustic comparability.
Specifically, one sentence was unique to the PIT ("Kik azok?"
['Who are they?']), and one was unique to the PRT ("Miért nem volt itt tegnap?"
['Why was he/she not here yesterday?']).
Sentences were systematically varied across syntactic structures: Declaratives (n=10), Questions (n=9), Imperatives (n=5), and Exclamations (n=5).
These were cross-matched with three Hungarian target intonation patterns: Sustained (n=10; e.g., "Bárcsak lenne testvérem!"
['If only I had a sibling!']), Descending (n=9; e.g., "A hétvégén moziban voltunk."
['We went to the movies this weekend.']), and Falling (n=9-10; e.g., "Indulj már a tízóraiért!"
['Go get your snack!']).
For the PIT, the reference audio was pre-recorded by two female, trained speech-language therapists using clear, expressive intonation.
The PRT evaluated how children applied prosodic features when decoding text, without the aid of an auditory model.
The 29 sentences were presented visually on a computer screen one by one, centered in an 88-point Calibri font on a solid grey background.
Participants were instructed to read the sentences aloud at a natural pace; a new sentence appeared immediately after they finished reading the current one.
Prosodic Imitation Task (PIT).
The PIT measured the child's maximum articulatory capacity, providing a child-specific benchmark for the objective acoustic analysis.
In this condition, auditory stimuli were presented via headphones, while the corresponding text was simultaneously displayed on the screen using the same visual parameters as the PRT.
Participants were instructed to repeat each sentence aloud after the auditory playback.

To prevent auditory priming or memory trace effects from influencing the children's natural reading prosody, task administration followed a fixed sequential order for all participants: the PRT was always administered prior to the PIT.
During the testing sessions, visual stimuli were presented in full-screen mode on a 15-inch laptop using Microsoft PowerPoint.
Instructions for the PRT were presented on-screen and read by the children, whereas the examiner explicitly read the on-screen instructions aloud prior to the PIT.
Before commencing the 29 experimental trials, each task began with a practice phase consisting of three identical sentences: "Miért?"
['Why?'], "Mi az ebéd ma?"
['What is for lunch today?'], and "Anyukám bolti eladó, apukám villamosvezető."
['My mom is a shop assistant, my dad is a tram driver.'].
These practice items were designed to familiarize the children with the procedure and covered different target intonation contours (falling, descending, and sustained, respectively).
Audio recordings from the practice phase were excluded from all subsequent acoustic analyses.
Continuous audio recording was maintained throughout the entire administration of both tasks using the Windows Voice Recorder application.
The children's vocal responses were captured using a headset microphone.
All automated acoustic pre-processing and feature extraction were performed using Python (Version 3.13.5; Python Software Foundation, 2025).
The raw, continuous audio recordings of both the reading and imitation tasks were segmented into sentence-level audio files using an automated pipeline.
First, the recordings were transcribed with timestamps using the OpenAI Whisper neural network model (large-v2; Radford et al., 2023).

text.text: To accurately isolate the target sentences, the generated transcriptions were aligned with the predetermined reference text using fuzzy string matching (via the rapidfuzz Python library).
Sentences were extracted from the continuous audio based on the matched timestamps, applying a padding of 0.25 seconds before and 0.70 to 1.0 seconds after the utterances.

For the imitation task, where the recordings contained both the adult model's prompt and the child's repetition, the audio files were split at the midpoint, retaining only the child's response for further analysis.
To ensure the reliability of the segmentation, a subset of the extracted audio files was manually audited to confirm boundary accuracy.

text.text: To quantify prosodic competence, each child's reading performance was mapped against their own Imitation Baseline for each sentence.
Four scores were computed:
The quotient of the total reading duration divided by the total imitation duration (DurationReading /DurationImitation ).
Values greater than 1.0 indicate temporal slowing and reduced processing speed during reading compared to their imitation baseline.
The frequency of syntactically inappropriate pauses.

While studies have conventionally defined pauses as acoustic silences falling within a 100 to 3,000 ms interval (Benjamin & Schwanenflugel, 2010; Chung & Bidelman, 2022; Miller & Schwanenflugel, 2008), this lower temporal threshold (100 ms) is highly susceptible to capturing natural phonetic closures, particularly given the slower articulation rates typical of pediatric populations.

text.text: We optimized the temporal threshold to 150 ms.

Furthermore, an automated relative energy threshold was implemented: a pausal intrusion was acoustically identified only if the root-mean-square (RMS) energy fell below 4% of the segment's maximum energy for a continuous duration of ≥ 150 ms.
The final metric was calculated by subtracting the number of baseline imitation pauses from the reading pauses.
Because reading and imitation naturally unfold at different temporal rates, standard linear comparisons (e.g., point-by-point correlations) of acoustic contours are mathematically unfeasible.
Therefore, we applied the Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithm (Senin, 2008), which non-linearly aligns two time-series sequences to find the optimal match, minimizing the distance between them.
text.formatted: Therefore, we applied the Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Senin, 2008)</ref>, which non-linearly aligns two time-series sequences to find the optimal match, minimizing the distance between them.

text.text: The alignment was implemented via the librosa Python library.
Breakdowns in sentence-level intonation representing the alignment distance (DTW cost) between the fundamental frequency (F0 ) contours of reading and its corresponding imitation baseline.
F0 contours were resampled to a fixed length of 50 data points, in order to capture structural contour shape.
To ensure the comparison reflects the true melodic shape rather than absolute pitch differences, the contours were z-score standardized prior to analysis.
DTW non-linearly warps the reading contour along the time axis to find the optimal alignment path.
The final cost was normalized by the alignment path length.
Higher scores indicate greater deviation from the target intonation.
Deviations in stress and syllabic rhythm.
Continuous intensity contours (dB) were extracted, resampled to 50 data points, and z-score standardized.
It is calculated as the path-normalized DTW distance between the standardized amplitude envelopes (intensity contours) of the two recordings.
Higher scores indicate greater deviation from the target rhythmic stress pattern.

text.text: To investigate the directional and mediational relationships between foundational cognitive skills (PA, RAN), acoustic-prosodic markers, and reading fluency, a path analysis was conducted with full information maximum likelihood (FIML) estimation.

Given the relatively small sample size for structural equation modeling, the path analysis was conducted as an exploratory approach to investigate the potential structural relationships between cognitive skills, prosodic markers, and reading fluency.
The path model demonstrated an excellent fit to the data.
The chi-square test was non-significant, indicating that the model did not significantly deviate from the observed data structure (χ²(7) = 7.97, p = .335).
Furthermore, all indices indicated excellent model fit (CFI = .995, TLI = .985, RMSEA = .050, SRMR = .054).
Given the small sample size, a post-hoc power and sensitivity analysis was conducted using the semPower package (Moshagen & Bader, 2024) to evaluate the model's capacity to detect misspecifications.
text.formatted: Given the small sample size, a post-hoc power and sensitivity analysis was conducted using the semPower package <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Moshagen & Bader, 2024)</ref> to evaluate the model's capacity to detect misspecifications.

text.text: Assuming a standard acceptable misfit (RMSEA = .08) and an alpha level of .05, the statistical power to reject a misspecified model with 7 degrees of freedom was low (1 -β = .16).
Further sensitivity analysis indicated that with N = 56, the current model only achieves adequate power (80%) to reliably detect large effect sizes (RMSEA ≥ .193).

Consequently, while the descriptive fit indices suggest an excellent model fit, the non-significant chi-square statistic should be interpreted with caution due to limited statistical power, which reinforces the exploratory nature of investigating these structural relationships.

text.text: The present study set out to examine (1) the extent to which objective acoustic markers of reading prosody predict reading fluency beyond the contribution of phonological awareness (PA) and rapid automatized naming (RAN), (2) whether PA and RAN relate to reading fluency directly or indirectly through children's acoustic prosodic execution, and (3) which specific acoustic dimensions of prosody carry the greatest explanatory weight.
Acoustic markers of reading prosody, specifically temporal features, were found to predict reading fluency beyond the contribution of cognitive markers.
Tempo stability emerged as the strongest direct predictor, whereas melodic and rhythmic markers did not account for any additional unique variance once temporal features were controlled for.
PA and RAN related to reading fluency through distinct routes.
While RAN maintained a direct relationship with reading fluency, the contribution of PA was fully indirect, explained by children's acoustic prosodic execution.
Finally, among the acoustic dimensions, temporal markers carried the greatest explanatory weight within this mediating pathway.
Stronger PA reduced pausal intrusions, which in turn limited subsequent shifts in rhythmic execution.
These downstream effects supported tempo stability, which consequently predicted reading fluency.

Our finding that PA influences reading fluency entirely through an indirect, mediated pathway aligns with the developmental model proposed by Critten et al. (2021), although our cross-sectional data reflect concurrent relationships rather than developmental change over time.

text.text: Research relying on behavioral tasks, such as stress-judgment or rhythm-detection, has frequently reported direct effects.
In contrast, our objective measurement approach uncovers a sequential relationship instead.
Specifically, phonological skills appear to provide the segmental foundation required to reduce pausal intrusions, which in turn allows for temporal execution during reading.

Moreover, the predominance of temporal markers in our model diverges from much of the largely English-language literature, which may reflect the distinct rhythmic and prosodic character of Hungarian language.

Hungarian is a syllable-timed language with fixed stress that carries no lexically contrastive function -unlike English, where stress alone can shift meaning (e.g., record vs. reCORD; Wade-Woolley & Heggie, 2016), or Mandarin, where pitch does (Chung & Bidelman, 2022).

text.text: Because stress prominences in syllable-timed languages occur less frequently than in stress-timed languages, stress-based processing was expected to carry little weight for reading in Hungarian (Calet et al., 2015).

text.text: Our finding that temporal features predicted reading fluency most strongly is consistent with this prediction.

Within this Hungarian sample, prosodic execution in reading appeared to be driven mainly by sentence-level mechanisms, such as temporal execution, rhythmic phrasing, and pausing, rather than by pitch-or stress-based aspects.
This pattern may also help explain why melody error, the dimension most directly tied to pitch, contributed no significant unique variance in the current path analysis.
Previously, measuring reading prosody has relied mostly on subjective, human-rated scales (e.g.
MFS; Zutell & Rasinski, 1991).

text.text: The present study introduces a methodological advancement to better capture the realities of pediatric speech.

Previous spectrographic approaches have often relied on adult template models, correlating a child's prosodic contour against an averaged adult standard (Duong et al., 2011); however, because children's speech rate is slower and more variable than that of adults, such comparisons can introduce developmental confounds.
text.formatted: Previous spectrographic approaches have often relied on adult template models, correlating a child's prosodic contour against an averaged adult standard <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Duong et al., 2011)</ref>; however, because children's speech rate is slower and more variable than that of adults, such comparisons can introduce developmental confounds.

text.text: The present methodology addressed this by benchmarking each child's reading performance against their own prosodic imitation, produced during a separate task, rather than against an external adult standard.

This individualized approach was applied selectively: dynamic time warping was used to align the melody and rhythm measures against each child's own imitation baseline, whereas tempo stability and pausal intrusions were derived directly from the reading performance itself, without requiring this alignment.
Our findings carry implications for previous frameworks of prosody's role in literacy
Several limitations should be acknowledged.

First, the size of the current sample limits the statistical power available for detecting smaller effects, particularly within the path model, and constrains the generalizability of the pathway structure.
As confirmed by sensitivity analysis, a sample size of 56 children only provides adequate statistical power to reliably detect large structural misspecifications (RMSEA ≥ .193).
Consequently, the path model may lack the precision needed to capture smaller, yet theoretically meaningful pathways among the multiple cognitive and acoustic predictors.

Therefore,conclusions regarding the unique contribution of each prosodic marker and the specific indirect role of phonological awareness should be considered exploratory and require validation in adequately powered future cohorts.
Second, the sample consisted of a single, narrow age range (8-11 years) of typically developing children.

Because prosodic competence and reading fluency both follow prolonged developmental trajectories, the mediating role of pausal intrusions and temporal stability observed here may not generalize to younger, pre-literate children or to older, more fluent readers, nor to children with reading difficulties.
Third, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation of our results.
Because all data were collected at the same time point, the temporal ordering required to establish a mediation chain cannot be confirmed.

While our path model tests a directional sequence based on previous frameworks (e.g., Wood et al., 2009), the findings represent concurrent structural relationships rather than developmental mechanisms.

text.text: Future longitudinal studies are needed to establish the temporal progression of these skills.

Relatedly, because participants were already literate, their orthographic knowledge may have influenced performance on the phonological awareness measures themselves, rather than these measures reflecting a pre-literate skill (Castles & Coltheart, 2004 , as cited in Critten et al., 2021).

text.text: This raises a directionality concern that extends to the prosodic measures as well: because prosodic competence was assessed through oral reading rather than through spontaneous speech, it cannot be definitively established whether prosodic execution shapes reading fluency, or whether more fluent, automatized reading itself enables more accurate prosodic production during the task.

Finally, the ecological validity of using oral reading as an indicator for children's broader prosodic competence must be taken with careful consideration, as reading prosody is not identical to spontaneous speech.

Spontaneous speech typically exhibits greater pitch variability and more frequent end-of-sentence pitch rises to mark minor syntactic boundaries (Esser & Polomski, 1988 , as cited in Schwanenflugel et al., 2015), alongside more frequent pausing and less consistent stress marking (Howell & Kadi-Hanifi, 1991 , as cited in Schwanenflugel et al., 2015).

text.text: Children's oral reading may therefore reflect a narrower range of their overall prosodic competence than the present measures suggest.
Despite these limitations, the study has several methodological and theoretical strengths.

Most importantly, by benchmarking each child's reading against their own prosodic imitation rather than an adult baseline, the study achieved a level of measurement sensitivity that allowed individual-level acoustic differences to emerge as meaningful predictors of reading fluency.

Furthermore, the focus on Hungarian language provided a theoretically In conclusion, the present study demonstrates that objective, individually matched acoustic measures of reading prosody can reveal structure in the relationship between foundational cognitive skills and reading fluency that behavioral and group-level measures may obscure.
In Hungarian primary school children, phonological awareness influenced reading fluency entirely through prosodic execution, with temporal stability as the strongest predictor.
Overall, these findings highlight the importance of acoustically grounded, language-specific approaches to understanding how prosody supports the development of reading fluency.

text.text: The research questions are: To what extent do objective acoustic markers of reading prosody predict reading fluency in Hungarian primary school children, beyond the contribution of phonological awareness and rapid automatized naming?
RQ2: Do phonological awareness and rapid automatized naming relate to reading fluency directly, or indirectly through children's acoustic prosodic execution?
RQ3: Which specific acoustic dimensions of prosody (melodic, rhythmic, temporal, or pause-related) carry the greatest explanatory weight in this mediating pathway?
Method Participants Sixty healthy children participated in the study.
Participants were recruited from primary schools in Hungary.

The study was conducted as part of a broader research project titled "New Technologies in the Identification of Reading Difficulties and the Development of Modern Remedial Methods" at the Research Centre for Natural Sciences (MTA TTK).

Second, linear regression analyses were conducted to measure the individual, predictive capacity of each prosodic metric on reading fluency.

Regression diagnostic checks, including residual normality (Shapiro-Wilk test), independence of errors (Durbin-Watson test), and homoscedasticity (Breusch-Pagan test), were evaluated for all linear models.
Third, a hierarchical multiple regression analysis was conducted to determine the unique variance in reading fluency explained by the prosodic markers above the cognitive predictors.
Predictors were entered into the model in three steps.
Step 1 established the baseline model by entering the standardized literacy controls (PA and RAN).
Step 2 introduced the temporal and pause-related scores (Tempo Stability and Pausal Intrusions).

Finally, Step 3 introduced the melody and rhythm scores (Melody and Rhythm DTW Costs) to determine whether deviations in intonation and rhythmic patterning explained additional variance in reading fluency beyond the predictors already in the model.
Multicollinearity was evaluated across all steps using Variance Inflation Factors (VIF).

development.Within Wood et al.'s (2009)  conceptual model, prosodic competence has been proposed as a single mediating construct operating alongside vocabulary and morphological awareness.

Our results suggest that this mediating role is itself internally structured: rather than acting as a unitary pathway, prosodic competence appears to function as a chain of effects, in which pausal control shapes rhythmic accuracy, which then determines temporal stability.
Furthermore, our findings provide a nuanced, cross-linguistic perspective on the Reading Systems Framework (RSF;Wade-Woolley et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Furthermore, our findings provide a nuanced, cross-linguistic perspective on the Reading Systems Framework (RSF;<ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Wade-Woolley et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: While the RSF situates prosodic competence as a phonological component acting on the lexicon primarily through the mapping of lexical stress, the current study indicates that this word-level pathway is marginal in Hungarian, where stress carries no lexically contrastive function.

Instead, prosodic competence appears to influence reading fluency predominantly through sentence-level temporal mechanisms, suggesting that the lexical pathway proposed within the RSF may be highly specific to stress-timed languages, whereas in the Hungarian language context, suprasegmental processing appeared to rely more on temporal phrasing.

These findings point to several directions for future research.

Future cross-sectional and longitudinal research spanning pre-literate to fluent stages is required to resolve these directionality concerns and confirm whether the observed pathway (phonological awareness → pausal control → temporal stability) represents a true developmental trajectory.

Given that the present sample consisted of typically developing readers, future work should also examine whether this same pathway, and particularly the dominant role of temporal stability, holds among children with reading difficulties, where prosodic competence may follow a different pattern.
Finally, an important limitation of the current study is the lack of a cross-linguistic comparison group.

Because our conclusions are based on a single language and a specific age range, the proposed theoretical role of language rhythm (e.g., syllable-timed versus stress-timed typology) could not be directly tested.

Cross-linguistic replication in other syllable-timed or tonal languages would further help clarify whether the sentence-level, temporal weighting observed in Hungarian reflects a broader typological principle or a language-specific pattern unique to Hungarian's stress system.
